# app-builder

**A shared build kit that turns a static web app into two offline deliverables: a portable Windows EXE and an Android APK.**

[![Landing page](https://img.shields.io/badge/landing%20page-open-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-builder/)
[![All projects](https://img.shields.io/badge/All%20projects-hub-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/)
[![Offline](https://img.shields.io/badge/offline-yes-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-builder)
[![Type: shared build kit](https://img.shields.io/badge/type-shared%20build%20kit-586069?style=flat-square)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-builder/)
[![Tech: Python + Kotlin](https://img.shields.io/badge/tech-Python%20%2B%20Kotlin-3572A5?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-builder)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-2e7d32?style=flat-square)](LICENSE)

**Landing page:** <https://drsamonline.github.io/app-builder/>  ·  **All projects:** <https://drsamonline.github.io/>


A small, reusable kit that turns a **static web app** into two double-clickable,
offline deliverables:

* a **single-file portable Windows EXE** (`<app>-portable.exe`) — a tiny Python
  launcher bundled with the app that serves it locally and opens the browser; and
* an **Android APK** (`<app>.apk`) — a dependency-free WebView wrapper of the
  same app.

Both work fully offline. A consuming app repo adds **one workflow file** and
gets freshly-built artifacts attached to a GitHub Release on every push.

---

## What's in here

```
exe/
  launcher.py        # serves the bundled app/ on 127.0.0.1 and opens a browser
  build.py           # PyInstaller --onefile build -> dist/<APP_NAME>-portable.exe
  requirements.txt   # pyinstaller
apk/
  settings.gradle.kts
  build.gradle.kts   # AGP 8.x + Kotlin plugin (apply false)
  gradle.properties
  app/
    build.gradle.kts            # compileSdk 34 / minSdk 24 / targetSdk 34, signed release
    src/main/AndroidManifest.xml
    src/main/java/com/drsamonline/appbuilder/MainActivity.kt
    src/main/res/values/strings.xml        # app label (placeholder, replaced by the workflow)
    src/main/assets/www/                    # <-- the app's HTML is copied here by the workflow
keystore/
  debug.keystore     # shared debug-grade signing key (see below)
tools/
  verify_exe.py      # inspects the built EXE: valid PE, executable, size budget, imports
examples/
  build-apps.yml     # the workflow a consuming repo drops into .github/workflows/
README.md
```

---

## How a repo uses the kit

Add `examples/build-apps.yml` as `.github/workflows/build-apps.yml` in your app
repo and set the three values under `with:` to match your layout:

```yaml
jobs:
  app:
    uses: drsamonline/app-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@main
    with:
      app_name: my-app        # -> my-app-portable.exe and my-app.apk
      app_src: docs/play      # folder containing your index.html (+ any assets)
      deploy_path: docs       # folder to publish to Pages ("" = do not deploy)
```

**Call the workflow; do not copy it.** The build, release and deploy live in the
reusable workflow, so a fix there reaches every app at once. An earlier
hand-copied version of this file drifted and kept `if: always()` on the release
job, which *deleted* the published release before recreating it.

The reusable workflow runs, on every push to `main` (and on manual
`workflow_dispatch`):

1. **`exe` job** (`windows-latest`) checks out your repo **and** this kit, copies
   `app_src/` into `exe/app/`, runs `python exe/build.py`, and uploads
   `<app_name>-portable.exe`.
2. **`apk` job** (`ubuntu-latest`) checks out both, installs the Android SDK
   packages, copies `app_src/` into `apk/app/src/main/assets/www/`, and runs
   `gradle assembleRelease` to produce a signed `<app_name>.apk`.
3. **`version` job** consumes any `changes/` files and bumps `VERSION` and
   `CHANGELOG.md`.
4. **`release` job** publishes both artefacts on a single fixed-tag release
   (`app-latest`) — created **only if it is missing**, then uploaded with
   `--clobber`. It never deletes the release first, so a failed build leaves the
   previous one intact.
5. **`pages` job** deploys `deploy_path` after the release lands.

A push that touches only root docs/meta (`*.md`, `LICENSE`, `.gitignore`, …) is
skipped entirely by `paths-ignore`, so a docs-only commit does not run the
builder.

### Stable download URLs

Because the tag is always `app-latest` and is recreated each run, these URLs are
permanent:

```
https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<APP_NAME>-portable.exe
https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<APP_NAME>.apk
```

Link your landing page to those and the download always tracks the latest build.

---

## The EXE launcher

`launcher.py`:

* picks a free port on `127.0.0.1`,
* serves the bundled `app/` folder with `http.server`,
* opens the user's default browser at the URL, prints it, and
* runs until the console window is closed / `Ctrl+C`.

It resolves its bundled data via `sys._MEIPASS` when frozen by PyInstaller, and
falls back to the script directory when run as a plain script.

`build.py` builds the EXE with `--onefile`, names it `<APP_NAME>-portable`, and
bundles the app folder as `app`. It uses the correct `--add-data` separator for
the platform (`;` on Windows, `:` elsewhere). Set `APP_NAME` in the environment
before running it.

Every build **inspects the EXE before it ships it.** `tools/verify_exe.py` reads
the PE and asserts it is a valid PE, an executable, within a size budget, and
imports nothing unexpected — then prints the machine, subsystem, size and imports
to the build log, so the record shows what actually shipped. `MAX_EXE_MB`,
`REQUIRED_IMPORTS` and `FORBIDDEN_IMPORTS` (and `SIGNED_REQUIRED=1`) tune the
assertions per app.

---

## The Android APK

The `apk/` project is deliberately minimal and dependency-free (platform
framework only — **no AndroidX**):

* `compileSdk 34`, `minSdk 24`, `targetSdk 34`, AGP 8.x.
* `MainActivity` is a full-screen `WebView` with JavaScript and DOM storage
  enabled, loading `file:///android_asset/www/index.html`.
* The hardware back button navigates the WebView history first.
* `INTERNET` permission is declared (some wrapped apps fetch remote assets).

The app's HTML lives in `app/src/main/assets/www/` — the workflow copies your
`docs/play/` folder there before building. The app label comes from
`res/values/strings.xml`; the workflow replaces the `APP_NAME_PLACEHOLDER`
token with `APP_NAME`.

---

## Signing key (read this)

`keystore/debug.keystore` is a **debug-grade** key (alias `androiddebugkey`,
store/key password `android`, CN=Android Debug, validity ~10000 days).

* Its only purpose is so that **successive builds can be installed over each
  other** during sideloading/iteration.
* It is **NOT** a Play-Store signing key. Do **not** publish to Google Play
  with it. It is public in this repository, so it provides no security.
* To use your own key, add repository **secrets** and pass them through in the
  `apk` job's environment:

  | secret | meaning |
  | --- | --- |
  | `KEYSTORE_FILE` | path to the keystore file you stage in the job |
  | `KEYSTORE_PASSWORD` | store password |
  | `KEY_ALIAS` | key alias |
  | `KEY_PASSWORD` | key password |

  `app/build.gradle.kts` reads those env vars and falls back to the committed
  debug key when they are unset.

---

## Caveats

* The APK is **debug-signed** (see above) — fine for sideloading, not for Play.
* The EXE is unsigned, so Windows SmartScreen may warn on first run
  ("More info" → "Run anyway"). Code-signing is out of scope for this kit.
* Each run costs ~2 GitHub-hosted runner-minutes (Windows + Linux). A cold
  Android build is the slower half (SDK + Gradle download).

# Clip Loom ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **Clean it before you paste it — with programs you can read.** [![Live demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-clean%20a%20link-b4482f?style=flat-square&labelColor=231d16)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-clip-loom/) [![Test](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/app-clip-loom/test.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=tests&labelColor=231d16)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-clip-loom/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Build + deploy](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/app-clip-loom/build-apps.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=build&labelColor=231d16)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-clip-loom/actions/workflows/build-apps.yml) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/drsamonline/app-clip-loom?style=flat-square&labelColor=231d16&color=b4482f)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-clip-loom/releases/latest) [![Licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-4f7a5c?style=flat-square&labelColor=231d16)](LICENSE) [![Built on the Loom](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20on-the%20Loom%20(app--jacquard)-b4482f?style=flat-square&labelColor=231d16)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard) [**Open the tool →**](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-clip-loom/)
![Clip Loom](docs/shot.png) A link with eleven tracking parameters. Text pulled out of a PDF with three spaces between every word. A paragraph going into a field that will not wrap. Clip Loom does those jobs with **programs you can read in full** — twenty lines of Weft-8 assembly each, running on a machine that lives in the page. ## The five programs | Program | What it does | The idea it uses | |---|---|---| | **Strip the query string** | cut a URL at the `?` | compare each byte with `0x3F`, stop when it matches | | **Squeeze runs of spaces** | `a b` → `a b` | remember the *previous* byte in a register and compare | | **Wrap at 40 characters** | insert a newline every 40 | count down in a register and refill it — the same code for any length | | **Strip query and fragment** | cut at `?` and at `#` | two terminators instead of one | | **One line per sentence** | newline after every `.` | one more comparison in the copy loop | Every program reads one byte at a time from the `CLIPBOARD` port, decides, and writes. No regular expressions, no library, nothing you cannot follow with a pencil. ## Built on the Loom This app does not carry its own computer. `docs/play/weft8.js` is the **Weft-8** from [Jacquard (the Loom)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard) — byte for byte the same engine, the same one its 102 assertions cover. What this repository adds is a host: a clipboard that hands the machine one byte at a time and collects what it writes. That is the whole design. The machine is shared; the job is a peripheral. ## Run it Open `docs/index.html`, or use the [live demo](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-clip-loom/). The Windows EXE and Android APK are on the [rolling release](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-clip-loom/releases/latest). Your text never leaves the tab: the machine reads it in the page, and the clipboard buttons use the browser's own clipboard API with a plain "select and copy" fallback if the browser refuses. ## Test it ``` npm install node test-node.js # 66 assertions — the machine and every program node tests/page-smoke.js # 9 assertions — the page, driven in jsdom ``` The program suite runs **every example each program ships** on the real machine, then the edges: the empty clipboard, text with no `?`, a run of five spaces, and a 120-character paragraph that must wrap into four lines with no character lost. It also checks the programs **bite**: delete the `?` comparison from program 01 and the example that says the query must go starts failing. ## The Weft-8 family One machine, seven faces. Every one of these runs `weft8.js` from the Loom, byte for byte — learn it once and you have learned all seven. | | what it is | |---|---| | [the Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/) | the machine and its editor — where it all starts | | [Weft Puzzles](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-weft-puzzles/) | five puzzles solved in assembly, a robot on a grid | | **Clip Loom** (you are here) | clipboard programs you can read: strip, squeeze, wrap | | [Weft-8 on hardware](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-hardware/) | the same machine in C, three-way parity with the JS one | | [weft8-kit](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-kit/) | rules small enough to sign off | | [Weft-8 Classroom](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-classroom/) | eight exercises that teach how a computer works | | [Weft-8 beside x86 and ARM](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-compare/) | the same four jobs in three machines | ## Licence **PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0** · © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin. Free for any noncommercial purpose.

# Companion Forge

<!-- shot:start -->

![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

<!-- shot:end -->

[![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-companion-forge/)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE)
[![download](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/drsamonline/app-companion-forge

**The drsamonline Forge system in your pocket.** The build queue, the state, the
kit dependency graph and the repo fleet — in one offline page. No accounts, no
network, no telemetry.

Built with **Forge** on the shared **web-kit** (storage, i18n EN/HI/GU, CSV, theme, a11y).

## What it does

Open the console and you get the whole system at a glance:

- a **summary** — items done, queue remaining, kits live, fleet size, average
  conformance score, blocked items;
- the **build queue** — every item with its kit dependencies, status and whether
  it is runnable right now;
- the **kit graph** — each kit with its consumer apps;
- the **repo fleet** — role, conformance score and visibility.

Search any view, export it to CSV, switch language (English / हिन्दी / ગુજરાતી) and
theme. Everything is local; the app never calls the network.

## Run it

Open `docs/play/index.html` in a browser. That's the whole app — the engine
(`docs/play/forge.js`), the bundled snapshot (`docs/play/data.js`) and the shared
runtime (`docs/play/web-kit.js`) sit next to it, so it works from `file://` and
from GitHub Pages.

```
node test-node.js      # 30 passed, 0 failed
```

## How it is built

The app is **thin**: all the common behaviour (storage, languages, CSV, theme,
accessibility) comes from **web-kit**; the only app-specific code is

- `docs/play/forge.js` — a small, pure, zero-dependency engine that reads the
  snapshot: `statusOf`, `isRunnable`, `nextRunnable`, `summarize`, the row
  builders, `search` and `toCSV`. It runs unchanged in the browser and under Node,
  so it is unit-tested headlessly;
- `docs/play/data.js` — a read-only snapshot generated from `forge` and `registry`
  by `gen_data.py`. It is bundled, never fetched.

## Build the EXE and APK

This repo calls the shared build workflow. On every push, GitHub Actions builds a
portable Windows EXE and a signed Android APK from `docs/play` and attaches them
to the `app-latest` release.

## Licence

MIT. (c) 2026 Dr Sohil Momin. Part of the Forge system — apps open, orchestrator licensed.

<!-- shot:start -->

![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

<!-- shot:end -->


<!-- badges:start -->

[![Source](https://img.shields.io/badge/Source-GitHub-0b1220?logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-encrypted-case-log)

[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-PolyForm_Noncommercial_1.0.0-blue)](LICENSE)
[![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/Dependencies-none-success)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-encrypted-case-log)
[![Offline ready](https://img.shields.io/badge/Offline-ready-success)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-encrypted-case-log)
[![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/drsamonline/app-encrypted-case-log/total)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-encrypted-case-log/releases)
[![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/drsamonline/app-encrypted-case-log)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-encrypted-case-log/commits/main)
<!-- badges:end -->


**Per-patient clinical notes, encrypted on the device. Offline. No account, no server.**

Everything lives on the device, encrypted at rest with **AES-256-GCM** (Web Crypto), in
**IndexedDB**. The page carries `connect-src 'none'`, so an outbound request is impossible
even by accident — there is nothing to send your notes to.

Built with Forge, composing five shared kits: `crypto-kit` (AES-GCM, PBKDF2, key wrap),
`case-kit` (the record shape), `search-kit` (ranked search), `export-kit` (save a file) and
`web-kit` (shell, storage runtime, PWA).

## Run it

Open `index.html` — that is the whole app. No build step, no install.

```
node tests/self-tests.js      # 15 tests, no browser needed
```

## The vault, and what it means for you

- You set a **passphrase**. A key-encryption key is derived from it with
  **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 600,000 iterations, a random 16-byte salt**.
- A random **data-encryption key (DEK)** encrypts the records. The passphrase only
  **wraps** the DEK — so changing the passphrase never re-encrypts a record.
- A **verifier** (a known constant encrypted with the DEK) makes a wrong passphrase fail
  cleanly instead of silently producing garbage.
- A **24-word recovery code** wraps the same DEK, so a forgotten passphrase is survivable.
  It is shown **once**.

> **Without the passphrase or the recovery code, the data is unrecoverable.** There is no
> server to reset it, and that is the point — not an oversight.

## The records

One record per blob, a **fresh 96-bit IV every time**, and the record id as **AAD**, so a
record cannot be swapped or replayed. The self-tests prove that: a swapped record fails to
decrypt, no IV is ever reused, and the ciphertext never contains the plaintext.

A patient carries a **short label — initials or a code, not a full name**. The device may be
shared, and the label is the field most likely to be seen.

## Search, and its ceiling

**You cannot search ciphertext.** On unlock the app decrypts every record into memory and
builds a transient index with `search-kit`; the index is thrown away on lock. A plaintext
index on disk would leak exactly what we encrypted, so there isn't one.

**The honest ceiling is about 50,000 records** — the decrypt-everything-on-unlock step is
linear, and past that the unlock becomes slow on a phone. It is not unlimited, and the app
does not pretend it is.

## Export and import

- **`.ecl`** — a single encrypted archive (the vault header and every encrypted record). It is
  already encrypted, so it is safe to keep anywhere.
- **Plaintext CSV** — behind a clear warning, for when you must hand something over.
- Import **decrypts first**, then hands the plaintext to `case-kit`'s interchange
  (`Case.importRecord`), so a record made here can be read by the family of clinical apps.

The round-trip is tested: **export → wipe → import → identical data.**

## Safety

Never persists the DEK; it is held in memory only and cleared on lock. **Auto-locks after 5
minutes idle** and on demand. Requests `navigator.storage.persist()` so the database is not
evicted.

# Image Toolkit

<!-- shot:start -->

![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

<!-- shot:end -->

[![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-image-toolkit/)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-informational)](LICENSE)

**Resize, compress, convert and strip the GPS out of a photo — on your device, with nothing uploaded.**

Every other "compress my image" page uploads the photo first. This one cannot: there
is no server, no account and no network request. The file is read into memory,
processed by the code in this repository, and written back out.

## What it does

| | |
|---|---|
| **Resize** | contain inside a box, aspect kept, never upscaled, never rounded to zero |
| **Compress** | the highest quality that still fits a byte budget — the search is six encoder calls, not a guess |
| **Convert** | JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF and BMP in; JPEG, PNG or WebP out |
| **Strip** | EXIF, XMP, IPTC, JPEG comments; PNG `eXIf`/`tEXt`/`iTXt`/`zTXt` |
| **Say what happened** | before → after bytes, the percentage, the dimensions, and whether a GPS block was found and removed |

The pixels are never touched by the strip: everything from the JPEG scan onwards is
kept byte for byte, and the PNG colour and image chunks are copied whole.

## The done-means, as the spec states it

> A 4 MB photo is resized and compressed to under 500 KB without any network request.

`node test-node.js` proves the two halves separately and honestly: the budget search
is driven by a fake encoder whose output shrinks with quality (the way a real one
does), so "4 MB → under 500 KB" is a real assertion about the search; and the page is
checked to call no `fetch`, open no `XMLHttpRequest` and load nothing external. What
the test cannot prove is how a real browser's canvas encoder sizes a real photo — that
is the browser's answer, and the app reports the size it actually got.

## When things go wrong

- **Bad input** — a file that is not an image is refused with the type it reported; a
  photo whose EXIF cannot be read is still processed, and the app says the metadata
  could not be read, so nobody assumes the GPS was stripped.
- **No network** — nothing changes; the app never had one.
- **Storage full or the download refused** — the button says the file was not written
  and why; the image stays in memory.
- **Corrupt or truncated file** — the browser's decoder refuses it and the app says so
  rather than showing a smaller picture.
- **HEIC** — named as something a browser cannot draw, not silently skipped.

## Run it

    node test-node.js          # the proof: 73 assertions, no dependencies
    python3 -m http.server -d docs 8000   # then open http://localhost:8000/play/

There is no build step. `docs/play/` is the app.

## Layout

    docs/index.html        the landing page
    docs/play/index.html   the app
    docs/play/imgtool.js   the engine — sniff, dimensions, EXIF, strip, fit, budget
    docs/play/web-kit.js   vendored, unmodified
    docs/play/export-kit.js vendored, unmodified
    test-node.js           the proof

## Licence

commercial use needs a paid licence. The engine file is MIT, as its header says.

# Jacquard ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **The loom you program — an 8-bit machine you can hold in your head.** [![Live demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-drsamonline.github.io%2Fapp--jacquard-d98324?style=flat-square&labelColor=1a1610)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/) [![Test](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/app-jacquard/test.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=tests&labelColor=1a1610)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Build + deploy](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/app-jacquard/build-apps.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=build&labelColor=1a1610)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard/actions/workflows/build-apps.yml) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/drsamonline/app-jacquard?style=flat-square&labelColor=1a1610&color=d98324)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard/releases/latest) [![Licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-3f7a52?style=flat-square&labelColor=1a1610)](LICENSE) [![Offline](https://img.shields.io/badge/network-none-3f7a52?style=flat-square&labelColor=1a1610)](#-what-it-refuses-to-do) [![No runtime dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/runtime%20deps-0-d98324?style=flat-square&labelColor=1a1610)](package.json) [**Open the loom →**](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/) · [Reference card](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/play/#card) · [What it refuses](#-what-it-refuses-to-do) · [Tests](#-the-proof)
--- Automation usually hides behind coloured boxes. Jacquard puts a **real machine** underneath it: a fictional 8-bit CPU, the **Weft-8**, programmed in assembly, with the clock, the calendar, the clipboard and the accelerometer exposed as **memory-mapped peripherals**. You read a register, you act on it — and you can watch every register, flag and byte change while it runs. The whole app is one page and two files it carries with it. No build step, no framework, no network, no account.
``` IN OFFICE_INSIDE ; read the machine's senses CMP R0, R15 JNZ done ; already at the office -> say nothing IN NEXT_EVENT_MIN CMP R1, R2 ; ten minutes or less? JG done OUT NOTIFY ; leave now done: HLT ```
## Contents | | | |---|---| | [The machine](#-the-machine) | the ISA, the flags, the memory map | | [What a program looks like](#-what-a-program-looks-like) | `leave-now`, end to end | | [The proof](#-the-proof) | 118 assertions: 102 for the engine, 16 that drive the page | | [What it refuses to do](#-what-it-refuses-to-do) | the failure behaviour, asserted not promised | | [Run it](#-run-it) | from a USB stick, a laptop, a phone | | [One honest note on the count](#-one-honest-note-on-the-count) | 27 opcodes, not 28 | ## The machine | | | |---|---| | **Registers** | 16 × 8-bit. `R0` is the accumulator — `LDI`, `LOAD` and `IN` all fill it, `MOV` moves it. | | **Flags** | `Z` zero · `C` carry/borrow · `N` negative · `V` signed overflow | | **Instructions** | fixed **two bytes**, little-endian: the opcode, then the operand | | **Operand** | an 8-bit value, address or port — or two registers packed as `a << 4 \| b` | | **Address space** | 256 bytes: ROM `0x00`–`0x7F`, RAM `0x80`–`0xBF`, peripherals `0xC0`–`0xFF` | | **Stack** | 16 deep, with overflow and underflow reported rather than crashed | Because the operand byte carries both registers, `ADD R12, R5` is literally `04 C5`. A program with a known listing assembles to exactly that listing, byte for byte — which is the first thing the tests assert. The peripherals are host callbacks, so the machine is testable with no browser at all: ``` CLOCK 0xC0 LAT 0xC1 LON 0xC2 OFFICE_INSIDE 0xC3 NEXT_EVENT_MIN 0xC4 NOTIFY 0xC5 CLIPBOARD 0xC6 ACCEL 0xC7 RNG 0xC8 AUDIO 0xC9 HALT 0xCA ``` ## What a program looks like `leave-now` ships with the app: notify ten minutes before the next calendar event, unless you are already at the office. It exercises a peripheral read, a comparison, a signed branch and an output — and all four of its paths are asserted. ``` IN OFFICE_INSIDE CMP R0, R15 ; R15 is 0 here JNZ done ; already there -> say nothing IN NEXT_EVENT_MIN MOV R1, R0 ; R1 = minutes to the event LDI 10 MOV R2, R0 ; R2 = 10 CMP R1, R2 JG done ; more than 10 minutes -> wait LDI 1 OUT NOTIFY ; leave now done: HLT ``` The page shows you the registers, the four flags, the program bytes, scratch RAM, and a **weave strip** that lights up the instruction the program counter is standing on. ## The proof ``` node test-node.js # 102 assertions, no dependencies — the engine node tests/page-smoke.js # 16 assertions — the page, driven in jsdom ``` The tests run the **real** engine — `docs/play/weft8.js`, the same file the page loads. Nothing is mocked except the peripherals, which are callbacks by design. - the encoding, byte for byte, including `ADD R12,R5` → `04 C5` - **all 27 opcodes** assembling and running in one program - **five hand-checked branch traces**, including signed `JL` at `-1` vs `1` and `JG` at `127` vs `-1`, where the subtract overflows - carry, overflow, zero and negative — from `ADD`, `SUB`, `SHL`, `SHR` **and `CMP`'s own borrow** - `CALL`/`RET` nesting, `PUSH`/`POP` order, the 16-deep overflow and the empty-stack `RET` - the peripherals, the ROM write refusal, the step limit, an opcode that does not exist - every refusal in the assembler, with the line number it refuses on - **the page itself**: that it loads the engine, that its script parses, and that every example it offers assembles on the machine it ships And `tests/page-smoke.js` boots the real page in jsdom, clicks the real buttons and reads the real DOM: run, step, reset, the weave strip, the device sliders reaching the machine, and a program that does not assemble being refused instead of run. That test exists because a page bug no engine test could see — `vm.h` where it should have been `vm.peripherals`, which made **Assemble & run** throw — shipped once and was caught only by driving the page. jsdom is a **test-only** dependency; the app has none. **Checked to bite**, not just to pass: rewrite `JL` to test `Z` and two branch traces fail; suppress `CMP`'s borrow and the carry assertion fails. ## What it refuses to do | Situation | What happens | |---|---| | The program does not assemble | it is **never run**; the error names the line and the reason — an undefined label, `R16`, an immediate of 300, a program past the 128-byte ROM | | The program loops forever | it stops at the step limit, and the page says it stopped there | | `RET` with an empty stack | an error, not a crash | | A write into ROM | refused **and reported**, rather than silently doing nothing | | Storage is full or unavailable | Save says so, and tells you to export instead; the editor keeps your program | | No network | nothing changes — there is nothing to fetch. The peripherals are simulated on the device | ## Run it Open `docs/index.html`. That is the whole app; `web-kit.js` and `weft8.js` sit next to it, so it works from `file://` and from GitHub Pages. | Where | How | |---|---| | **Browser** | [drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/) | | **Windows** | the portable EXE on the [rolling release](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard/releases/latest) | | **Android** | the signed APK on the same release | | **Anywhere** | copy the folder; there is nothing to install | ## One honest note on the count The spec asks for "a program using all **28** opcodes" and then names twenty-seven: `LDI MOV LOAD STORE ADD SUB AND OR XOR NOT SHL SHR CMP JMP JZ JNZ JG JL CALL RET PUSH POP IN OUT RAND NOP HLT`. The machine has **27**, and this README says so rather than inventing a twenty-eighth to satisfy a number. ## The Weft-8 family One machine, seven faces. Every one of these runs `weft8.js` from the Loom, byte for byte — learn it once and you have learned all seven. | | what it is | |---|---| | **the Loom** (you are here) | the machine and its editor — where it all starts | | [Weft Puzzles](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-weft-puzzles/) | five puzzles solved in assembly, a robot on a grid | | [Clip Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-clip-loom/) | clipboard programs you can read: strip, squeeze, wrap | | [Weft-8 on hardware](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-hardware/) | the same machine in C, three-way parity with the JS one | | [weft8-kit](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-kit/) | rules small enough to sign off | | [Weft-8 Classroom](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-classroom/) | eight exercises that teach how a computer works | | [Weft-8 beside x86 and ARM](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-compare/) | the same four jobs in three machines | ## Licence **PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0** · © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin. Free for any noncommercial purpose; commercial use needs a licence from the author.

# Lantern [![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-lantern/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-lantern/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE) [![node](https://img.shields.io/badge/node-%3E%3D18-339933)](package.json) [![dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/runtime%20dependencies-none-22c55e)](package.json) **A whole library, served over your own Wi-Fi, with no internet at any point.** One device — a laptop, a Raspberry Pi, a phone that can run Node — becomes a local content server. Everyone else on the same network opens the address it prints, in a **plain browser**, and browses, searches and reads a bundled library. Nothing leaves the host unless you export it. This is an "Internet-in-a-Box" as an app: a school, clinic or village gets a searchable library for the cost of one device and none of the connectivity. ## Run it ```bash node server.js # or: node server.js 8080 ``` It prints the addresses to open: ``` Lantern is serving 3 document(s) on port 8080 Open on any device on this Wi-Fi: http://192.168.1.24:8080/ No internet is used at any point. ``` Then, on the host, open the Packs card and import `examples/starter-pack.json`. Anyone on the Wi-Fi can now read and search it. There is nothing to install and nothing to build: the host is one Node file with **no dependencies**, and the client is one page with no build step. ## What it does - **Host mode.** Import content packs into the host; it serves them on the LAN. - **Client.** Anyone on the network opens the address in a browser — no app, no account, no internet. - **Search.** A full-text index over every document in every pack, built on the host. A document containing the whole query as a **phrase** outranks one that merely contains its words. - **Pack manager.** Each pack's **true byte size**, its document count, and one button to remove it — which removes its documents from search at once. - **Usage stays local.** No analytics, no call home, no third-party request in either the host or the page. ## A pack A pack is one JSON file: ```json { "id": "my-pack", "title": "My Pack", "docs": [ { "path": "notes.html", "title": "Notes", "content": "

Notes

" } ] } ``` On import Lantern writes each document and records its **SHA-256 and byte length** in the pack's own `manifest.json`. It re-checks both every time it loads a pack. ## When things go wrong | Situation | What Lantern does | |---|---| | A document path tries to leave the pack (`../`, an absolute path) | The import is refused and the path is named. A request for such a path is refused with 403. | | A file cannot be written (no space, read-only disk) | The pack is **not** added, the files that did not land are named, and nothing half-written is left behind — a reader cannot tell a missing page from a missing chapter. | | A pack's files no longer match its manifest | The pack is moved to `.quarantine/`, reported in the Packs card, and is neither served nor searchable. | | A bundle that is not JSON, or has no documents | Refused with the reason shown. | | No peers, no internet | Nothing changes: the library still opens on the host, and says how many documents it holds. | ## Tests ```bash node test-node.js # 49 passed, 0 failed ``` Every claim above is checked **over real HTTP against a real host**, because the point of a LAN app is that a browser on the network can read it. The suite covers: the host taking a port and answering, the client page being served, import and the true byte size read back off disk, a document read over HTTP, phrase-first ranking (ahead of documents that only carry the words), search after a pack is removed, traversal refusal, an unsafe bundle path, a bundle that is not JSON, a write that fails with `ENOSPC`, and a checksum mismatch being quarantined. The assertions were checked to **bite**: with the phrase bonus removed and both traversal guards removed, 10 of them fail. ## Built on - [lan-kit](https://github.com/drsamonline/lan-kit) — vendored as `public/lan-kit.js` for the LAN address helpers (`Lan.hostUrl`), so the page and the host agree on what address a phone should open. ## Licence PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 — see [LICENSE](LICENSE). © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin.

# Panchang

<!-- shot:start -->

![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

<!-- shot:end -->

[![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-panchang/)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE)

**A daily Indian almanac that runs entirely offline.** Tithi, nakshatra, yoga,
karana, paksha, vaara, sunrise, sunset, rahu-kaal, and a muhurat finder — computed
on your device from the date and your location. No accounts, no network, no
telemetry.

Built with **Forge** on the shared **web-kit** (storage, i18n, CSV, theme, a11y).

## What it does

Pick a date and a place (or tap **Use my location**). The app computes the day's
panchang: the tithi and its paksha, the nakshatra, yoga and karana, the sunrise
and sunset, and the Rahu Kaal window. It flags the day's observances (Purnima,
Amavasya, Ekadashi, Pradosh, Sankranti) and can list the next auspicious muhurat
windows. The whole month exports to CSV.

## Run it

Open `docs/play/index.html` in a browser. That's the whole app — the engine
(`docs/play/panchang.js`), the astronomy core (`docs/play/astro-kit.js`) and the shared runtime (`docs/play/web-kit.js`) sit
next to it, so it works from `file://` and from GitHub Pages.

```
node test-node.js      # 24 passed, 0 failed
```

## How the panchang is computed

Entirely on-device, from first principles:

- the apparent **solar and lunar ecliptic longitudes** use the low-precision
  method from Meeus, *Astronomical Algorithms* (ch. 25 & 47);
- **tithi** and **karana** come from the moon–sun elongation; **nakshatra** and
  **yoga** use a **Lahiri ayanamsa** (linear approximation);
- **sunrise / sunset** use the standard sunrise equation; **rahu-kaal** is the
  weekday's segment of the real sunrise-to-sunset day (so it is more accurate
  than the fixed 6-to-6 tables).

The engine is cross-checked against an independent ephemeris in `test-node.js`:
elongations agree to better than 0.05°, and sunrise/sunset to within a few
minutes. This is a **first pass** — accurate to a few minutes near a
tithi/nakshatra boundary. For ritual-critical use, verify against a printed
panchang for your city.

## Build the EXE and APK

This repo calls the shared build workflow. On every push, GitHub Actions builds a
portable Windows EXE and a signed Android APK from `docs/play` and attaches them
to the `app-latest` release.

## Licence

MIT. (c) 2026 Dr Sohil Momin. Part of the Forge system — apps open, orchestrator licensed.

# Poet's Studio

<!-- shot:start -->

![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

<!-- shot:end -->

[![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-poets-studio/play/)
[![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-poets-studio/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-poets-studio/actions/workflows/test.yml)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-informational)](LICENSE)
[![download](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/drsamonline/app-poets-studio

**Rhyme, metre and fixed forms — offline, no accounts, no telemetry.**

Poet's Studio is a workshop, not a generator. It measures the poem you wrote:
the metre as you type, the rhyme sound of every line ending, and whether a
sonnet, haiku or ghazal you are attempting actually is one. It never writes a
line for you.

Master list **#130** · built from `QUEUE/app-poets-studio.md`.

## What it does

- **Rhyme finder** — perfect, near and slant rhymes, found by *sound* from a
  pronouncing dictionary, with a syllable filter. Spelling is not consulted, so
  `though` and `cough` are correctly told apart and `say` rhymes with `away`.
- **Syllable and metre counter** — every line, with its stress pattern shown as
  a running bar. When the line is regular the metre is named (iambic pentameter,
  trochaic tetrameter, …); when it is not, it is not named.
- **Fixed forms as constraints that check you** — Shakespearean sonnet, haiku,
  ghazal, and a custom stanza with your own syllable counts and scheme. Each is
  a live pass/fail with the reason, per line.
- **Writing journal** — drafts, versions and notes, all on the device. Export one
  poem, the whole journal as JSON, or every draft as a ZIP.

## The three rhyme strengths

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **Perfect** | the same sound from the last stressed vowel | `wall` / `fall`, `day` / `grey` |
| **Near** | the same consonant frame, a different vowel | `cat` / `cot`, `love` / `move` |
| **Slant** | the same stressed vowel, a different ending | `cat` / `cap` |

## The dictionary, and its size

`docs/play/dict.js` carries the **CMU Pronouncing Dictionary** — **124,085
words**, one pronunciation each — inside the app, so rhyme and metre work with
no network and no model.

It ships in a single-character ARPAbet encoding (each phoneme is one printable
character at `33 + its index in Poetry.ALPHABET`), which is **1.9 MB of text
instead of 3.6 MB** and decodes in one pass. The tab that separates the word
from its phonemes is what marks a line as encoded, so a plain `word P1 P2`
dictionary can still be pasted in by hand.

The dictionary is BSD-2-Clause and its licence travels with it in
[NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md).

## What it refuses to do

- **Write the poem.** There is no generator, no prompt box, no suggestion engine.
- **Guess at a word it does not know.** An unknown word is named in the line
  and counted as one syllable, and the line is marked inexact — a metre count
  that is quietly wrong is worse than one that says it is unsure.
- **Call an irregular line regular.** A metre is only named when at least 60% of
  its feet fit; otherwise the pattern is shown and the name is left off.

## Run it

Open `docs/play/index.html`. That is the whole app — the kits and the dictionary
sit next to it, so it works from `file://` and from GitHub Pages.

```
node test-node.js      # 76 assertions, no dependencies
```

## How it is built

| | |
|---|---|
| `docs/play/index.html` | the app — one page, no build step |
| `docs/play/poetry.js` | the engine: syllables, stress, rhyme, metre, forms. Works in the browser and in Node, so the tests test the app |
| `docs/play/dict.js` | the bundled dictionary |
| `docs/play/web-kit.js` | shell, storage, theme, i18n, CSV |
| `docs/play/export-kit.js` | files and ZIP off the device |

The form checks are deliberately honest about the difference between a
*dictionary* stress and a *verse* stress: CMUdict marks `is` and `a` as primary
stressed, which no one beats in a line, so a sonnet line is allowed to depart
from the ideal pattern in up to 20% of its syllables rather than being held to a
perfection no real sonnet has.

## Licence

PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 — free for any noncommercial purpose. Commercial use
needs a licence from the author. See [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).

The bundled dictionary keeps its own **BSD-2-Clause** licence, and that licence
travels with it.

# Weft Puzzles ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **Six small programming puzzles, solved on a real 8-bit machine.** [![Live demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-play%20it-4fd1e0?style=flat-square&labelColor=0a2342)](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-weft-puzzles/) [![Test](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/app-weft-puzzles/test.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=tests&labelColor=0a2342)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-weft-puzzles/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Build + deploy](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/drsamonline/app-weft-puzzles/build-apps.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=build&labelColor=0a2342)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-weft-puzzles/actions/workflows/build-apps.yml) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/drsamonline/app-weft-puzzles?style=flat-square&labelColor=0a2342&color=4fd1e0)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-weft-puzzles/releases/latest) [![Licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-5ee0a0?style=flat-square&labelColor=0a2342)](LICENSE) [![Built on the Loom](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20on-the%20Loom%20(app--jacquard)-ffb454?style=flat-square&labelColor=0a2342)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard) [**Play it →**](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-weft-puzzles/) · [The machine it runs on](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard)
![Weft Puzzles](docs/shot.png) A robot on a grid, five puzzles, and a machine with sixteen registers, four flags and twenty-seven instructions — **and no `if` statement**. So you build one, out of `CMP` and `JZ`. That is the whole point of the puzzles: the constraint is the lesson. ## The six puzzles | # | Puzzle | What it teaches | |---|---|---| | 01 | **First thread** | `LDI` puts a number in the accumulator, `OUT MOVE` hands it to the machine | | 02 | **Step around** | four moves, three directions — a straight line is not always the answer | | 03 | **Until you stand on it** | `LOAD` reads a port; `CMP` + `JZ` are how a machine decides | | 04 | **Feel for the wall** | `BUMPED` is the machine's own feedback — a loop that reacts | | 05 | **The whole weave** | a level can ask for more than arrival: collect both flags first | | 06 | **The long way round** | three bump loops in a row — a program is a shape you repeat | Each puzzle ships a **working solution**, and the test suite runs every one of them on the real machine. A puzzle nobody has solved is a puzzle nobody knows is solvable — so that is asserted, not assumed. ## Built on the Loom This app does not carry its own computer. It runs the **Weft-8** from [Jacquard (the Loom)](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-jacquard) — `docs/play/weft8.js` is that engine, byte for byte the same file, and the same one its 102 assertions cover. What this repository adds is a *world*: `docs/play/world.js` puts the machine inside a grid and hangs seven ports off it, at `0xD0` and up so they never collide with the Loom's own `0xC0`–`0xCA`: ``` POS_X 0xD0 POS_Y 0xD1 UNDER 0xD2 MOVE 0xD3 BUMPED 0xD4 DONE 0xD5 BEEP 0xD6 ``` So the machine is unchanged, and the puzzle is a peripheral — which is exactly how a real 8-bit computer met the world. ## Run it Open `docs/index.html`, or play the [live demo](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-weft-puzzles/). Windows EXE and Android APK are on the [rolling release](https://github.com/drsamonline/app-weft-puzzles/releases/latest). ## Test it ``` npm install # jsdom, test-only node test-node.js # 69 assertions: the machine, the world, and every level's solution node tests/page-smoke.js # 12 assertions: the page, driven in jsdom ``` The engine suite asserts that the machine is still the Loom's (two-byte encoding, 27 opcodes), that the world obeys its own rules (walls refuse a move and set the bump flag, flags are taken once, the checker knows a level with a flag left is not solved), that **every level's reference solution solves it in under 400 steps and fits the 128-byte ROM**, and that wrong answers are refused — walking into the wall, stopping one square short, and guessing a corridor's length blind. The page suite boots the real page, picks puzzles, runs programs, peeks at the solution and checks the page says *Solved* — because a page that does not work is not a puzzle. ## The Weft-8 family One machine, seven faces. Every one of these runs `weft8.js` from the Loom, byte for byte — learn it once and you have learned all seven. | | what it is | |---|---| | [the Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-jacquard/) | the machine and its editor — where it all starts | | **Weft Puzzles** (you are here) | five puzzles solved in assembly, a robot on a grid | | [Clip Loom](https://drsamonline.github.io/app-clip-loom/) | clipboard programs you can read: strip, squeeze, wrap | | [Weft-8 on hardware](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-hardware/) | the same machine in C, three-way parity with the JS one | | [weft8-kit](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-kit/) | rules small enough to sign off | | [Weft-8 Classroom](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-classroom/) | eight exercises that teach how a computer works | | [Weft-8 beside x86 and ARM](https://drsamonline.github.io/weft8-compare/) | the same four jobs in three machines | ## Licence **PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0** · © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin. Free for any noncommercial purpose.

# art-kit [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-2e7d32)](LICENSE) **The art primitives Forge was missing.** Zero dependencies, one file, no assets. palette · pixel canvas · draw ops · undo · dithering · median-cut · sprite sheets · isometric · sketch loop
--- ## The two halves - **STATIC pixel art** — an indexed palette, a pixel canvas that scales with **nearest-neighbour** (smoothing off by default — the classic trap), draw ops, a delta undo stack, dithering, median-cut quantisation, sprite sheets, and the isometric mapping. - **LIVE generative visuals** — a frame loop (`Art.sketch`) you can run on its own or drive from `game-kit`'s fixed timestep, so a sketch is reproducible from a fixed step. Both, from one kit. ## What's in it | | | |---|---| | `palette` | an indexed palette from a Lospec-style list, with `swap`, `cycle` and `nearest` | | `canvas` | an indexed pixel buffer: `set`, `line`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `fill`, `mirror` | | `scale` | nearest-neighbour upscaling (never smooths) | | `history` | a bounded undo/redo stack that stores **deltas, not whole frames** | | `dither` | ordered (Bayer) and Floyd–Steinberg | | `quantize` | median-cut to N colours, so a photo becomes pixel art | | `spriteSheet` / `sliceSprite` | a sheet + JSON atlas, with a slicing round-trip | | `iso` | the cartesian ↔ isometric coordinate mapping | | `sketch` | a setup-once / draw-every-frame loop | ## Usage ```js var Art = require("./art-kit.js"); // Node; in a browser it is window.Art var pal = Art.palette("1a1c2c 5d275d b13e53 ef7d57"); // a Lospec-style list var c = Art.canvas(32, 32, pal); c.rect(4, 4, 24, 24, 2, true).ellipse(16, 16, 10, 10, 3, true); var big = Art.scale(c, 8); // nearest-neighbour, crisp var hist = Art.history(c, { limit: 100 }); // undo/redo over deltas hist.begin(); c.set(0, 0, 1); hist.commit(); hist.undo(); var pal2 = Art.palette(Art.quantize(pixels, 16)); // median-cut a photo var sheet = Art.spriteSheet([frame0, frame1]); // sheet + atlas ``` ## Licence position (read this) Everything here is **reimplemented from published technique**; permissive reference projects are named only in comments, and **no code is copied**. In the survey behind this kit: Aseprite is not open source (learn, never copy); Data-Pixels and pixel8 carry **no licence**; six tools are copyleft — none of their code is used. The permissive references (piskel, Pixelorama, PixelCraft, poxi, and the isometric mapping from isometric-contributions) are cited as ideas. ## Tests ``` node test-node.js 31 passed, 0 failed ``` Covers the spec's required cases — a **nearest-neighbour scaling** case, a **dithering pattern** case, a **median-cut** case with a known input, and a **sprite-sheet export round-trip** — plus the palette, every draw op, the bounded delta undo stack, the isometric mapping and the sketch loop. All headless. ## License PolyForm Noncommercial — see [LICENSE](LICENSE). © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin.

# astro-kit

[![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/astro-kit/)
[![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/astro-kit/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/astro-kit/actions/workflows/test.yml)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-blue)](LICENSE)

**The shared astronomy core for drsamonline apps.** Zero dependencies. The
primitives a **panchang** (Indian almanac) needs — and nothing app-specific:

- **Julian day**; **solar** and **lunar longitude** (Meeus);
- **ayanamsa** (Lahiri, approximate); **sunrise / sunset / solar transit**;
- **moon phase** and illumination;
- the derived **tithi, nakshatra, yoga, karana** — from the sun–moon longitude.

```js
const p = Astro.panchang({ y: 2026, m: 10, d: 23, h: 6 }, { lat: 28.6139, lon: 77.2090 });
p.tithi.name;        // "Shukla Dwadashi"
p.nakshatra.name;    // "Purva Bhadrapada"
p.sun.sunriseUTC;    // -> add your timezone offset
```

## Verified against published values

```
node test-node.js
13 passed, 0 failed
```

- Sun apparent longitude vs **Meeus 25.b**: `199.90894` (published `199.90895`).
- Moon longitude vs **Meeus 47.a**: `133.16000` (published `133.162655`).
- Delhi sunrise/sunset, midsummer: `05:24` / `19:22` IST.
- Tithi/nakshatra/yoga/karana ranges and the tithi–elongation relation.

## Accuracy — read this

Solar and lunar longitude are good to about **0.01–0.05°**, which puts a
tithi/nakshatra boundary within roughly **a minute of time**. So panchang
timings are **approximate** — do not present them as exact, and local tradition
may differ. The ayanamsa is a linear Lahiri approximation.

# audio-kit [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-2e7d32)](LICENSE) **Synthesis, theory, patterns and notation.** Zero dependencies, one file, no audio assets. synthesis · ADSR · filters · noise · mixer · music theory · patterns · notation · sonification · mastering
--- ## The rule this kit exists to state **Game music is PATTERNS, NOT FILES.** A Forge game ships as one file with no assets. A pattern is a few kilobytes of data and plays through WebAudio; an audio file is megabytes. `game-kit` should adopt this rule: generate the music, do not ship it. ## What's in it | | | |---|---| | `music` | notes, intervals, transposition, 12 scales, 11 chords — the arithmetic every musical feature needs | | `synth` | a pure **ADSR** envelope, an oscillator voice with an optional filter, a noise source, and a small mixer | | `seq` | a **pattern sequencer**: rows × channels of notes, flattened to timed events and scheduled through WebAudio | | `notation` | a staff **layout** — each note's position, so a renderer just draws it | | `sonify` | map the bytes of any file to sound | | `master` | **honest** mastering helpers: a loudness measure, a match gain, and a peak limiter | Everything is generated in code or stored as pattern data. **No audio assets are shipped.** ## Usage ```js var A = require("./audio-kit.js"); // Node; in a browser it is window.AudioKit // Theory — no audio needed A.music.scale("C4", "major"); // -> [60, 62, 64, 65, 67, 69, 71] A.music.chord("A4", "minor"); // -> [69, 72, 76] A.music.parse("A4").freq; // -> 440 // Synthesis — on a user gesture (the browser rule) var ctx = new AudioContext(); var v = A.synth.voice(ctx, { type: "square", freq: 440, filter: "lowpass", cutoff: 900 }); v.play(ctx.currentTime, 0.5, { a: 0.01, d: 0.1, s: 0.7, r: 0.3 }); // A pattern: a few KB of data, not a file var pat = A.seq.pattern([ ["C4", null, null, "E4"], ["G4", null, "B4", null] ], { bpm: 120, rowsPerBeat: 4 }); A.seq.play(ctx, pat, { type: "square" }); // Notation layout A.notation.layout(["C4", "D4", "E4"]); // -> { notes: [{x, step, ...}], width } ``` ## Notes - **No autoplay.** Every node is built from a context you create on a user gesture. - **Everything is reimplemented.** References (the tracker tradition, Orca, MuseScore, matchering, binary-synth, Neothesia) are named in comments; **no code is copied**, and the copyleft ones are technique only. - **The mastering helpers are a matching aid, not a replacement for an engineer** — say so in any app that uses them. ## Tests ``` node test-node.js 42 passed, 0 failed ``` Covers the spec's required cases — an **ADSR envelope shape**, a **scale/chord construction**, a **sequencer scheduling** case (notes land on the right beats), and a **notation layout** — plus note parsing, transposition, sonification and the mastering helpers. All headless: the theory, the envelope maths and the scheduling are pure, so they test with no audio context. ## License PolyForm Noncommercial — see [LICENSE](LICENSE). © 2026 Dr Sohil Momin.

# audit

[![Licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/licence-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-3f7a52

The change log for the drsamonline fleet — **78 repositories, 105 workflow files, 10 scheduled jobs**.

Every audit, fix and correction lands here, with the evidence. Nothing in this repo is a plan for
later; if it says a thing was done, the `log/` entry that claims it carries the before-and-after.

## Why this exists

The fleet grew faster than its bookkeeping. Licence badges drifted from their LICENSE files, new
repos fell into an "Other / New" bucket, landing pages stopped offering downloads, and the audit
files that documented all of it were scattered across five unrelated repos. This repo is the single
place where the state of the fleet is measured, the change is recorded, and the next run can prove
what moved.

## Layout

    log/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md   one file per session
    state/                             machine-readable snapshots, refreshed by tools/collect.py
    tools/collect.py                   read every repo into state/
    tools/diff.py                      compare two snapshots, print only what changed
    tools/licence_check.py             licence badge vs LICENSE file, all repos
    tools/fix_licence_badges.py        make a badge say what its LICENSE grants

## The rule

**A change is not done when it is pushed. It is done when it is read back from the API and the
batch's verification passes.** The log entry records the verification, not the intention.

Every log entry uses the same six headings, in this order:

    ## What I looked at
    ## What was wrong
    ## What I changed
    ## Evidence
    ## What I deliberately did not do
    ## Next

The fifth one matters most. A log that only records what changed hides the decisions that were
made by *not* changing something, and those are the ones that get re-litigated later.

## Read state through the API, never through raw

`raw.githubusercontent.com` serves a cached copy that lags minutes to hours behind a commit. In this
fleet it has twice made finished work look broken:

- a `build.yml` that already contained the icon wiring was served without it
- 14 landing pages that had just been repaired were served in their old, broken form

Both times the API (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}`) showed the truth immediately.
**Use the API to decide whether something worked.** Use raw only for bulk reading of files that
have not changed in the last hour. Where a URL matters, fetch actual bytes and check the status.

## Running it

    gh auth login                      # or GH_TOKEN in the environment
    python3 tools/collect.py           # ~5 minutes for 78 repos
    python3 tools/licence_check.py     # exits 1 if any badge is wrong

`licence_check.py` runs weekly on a Monday at 03:31 UTC and commits the fresh snapshot. That cron is
deliberately clear of every other job in the fleet — the current set is:

    Mon 03:17  update-profile        Mon 03:23  skills/refresh
    Mon 03:31  licence-check (this)  Tue 03:47  dashboard/refresh
    Tue 04:00  metrics               Tue 04:12  Matneo/blog
    Tue 04:22  Matneo/store          Tue 06:00  control-panel/scan
    Wed 05:00  app-builder/kit-tests 1st+16th 03:00 store-images, 03:37 refresh-hub

## Conventions

- **One commit per repo.** Repos are independent; there is no shared release train, and a
  cross-repo change cannot be reverted per repo.
- **A script fixes a class of defect; a human decides a class of question.** Encoding a space is
  a script. "Is this repo MIT or PolyForm?" is not.
- **Never let a sweep invent a licence.** If a badge and its LICENSE disagree, the sweep stops
  and the repo goes to the decision batch.
- **Test against the real response shape and the broken state.** Two repairs in this log failed
  because they were tested against cached data and against a clean page instead of the damaged one.

Licence: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 — see LICENSE.

# backup [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-2e7d32)](LICENSE) **Snapshot a repository before it changes — so a merge can never lose the code that was there.** A reusable GitHub workflow + a zero-dependency script. Compressed, timestamped, rotated, and never full.
--- ## What it does Before a merge replaces a repository's code, `backup` takes the **state that is about to be replaced** and stores it, compressed, in a **dumps** repository: ``` dumps/ drsamonline__ml-kit/ 2026-10-24T103000Z/ ml-kit.tar.gz 2026-10-24T110000Z/ ml-kit.tar.gz drsamonline__case-kit/ 2026-10-24T103000Z/ case-kit.tar.gz ``` One folder per repository (`owner__repo`), one folder per backup named with the **date and time**, and inside it the repository as a `.tar.gz`. ## The two rules that keep it safe 1. **It never fills up.** Each repository keeps the newest **100** backups (configurable). Past that, the **oldest is deleted** to make room for the new one — so the most recent work is always present and the store stays bounded. 2. **It never stops.** When a dumps repository passes its **size cap** (800 MB by default), the next one is **created automatically** — `dumps`, `dumps-2`, `dumps-3`, … — and the backup continues there. A full repo can never block a backup. ## How to wire it in — before every merge Add this to any repository's workflow. It runs on a pull request, so it snapshots the **base commit** — the code as it is *before* the merge: ```yaml name: backup on: pull_request: jobs: backup: uses: drsamonline/backup/.github/workflows/backup.yml@main with: keep: 100 # optional max_mb: 800 # optional secrets: BACKUP_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.BACKUP_TOKEN }} ``` One secret, **`BACKUP_TOKEN`**, is required: a token with `contents: write` on the dumps repositories and `contents: read` on the source repository. (`GITHUB_TOKEN` is scoped to a single repository, so it cannot write to the dumps repo.) Run it by hand too: ```bash GITHUB_TOKEN=... python3 backup.py --repo drsamonline/ml-kit --ref main GITHUB_TOKEN=... python3 backup.py --repo drsamonline/forge --ref main --dumps dumps --keep 100 ``` ## Read this before you make the dumps repo public **A dumps repository holds your source code.** If *any* repository you back up is private, its dumps must be private too — a public dumps repo would publish that code. `backup.py` therefore creates new dumps repos **private by default**; pass `--public` only when every source repository is already public. ## The options | flag | default | what it does | |---|---|---| | `--repo` | — | the source repo, `owner/name` | | `--ref` | the default branch | the ref to snapshot — pass the **PR base** to capture the pre-merge state | | `--dumps` | `dumps` | the dumps repo name | | `--owner` | the source owner | who owns the dumps repo | | `--keep` | `100` | backups kept per repository; the oldest beyond it are deleted | | `--max-bytes` | `800 MB` | the dumps repo size cap before rolling to a new repo | | `--public` | off | create new dumps repos public (read the warning above) | | `--restore-test` | — | do not back up: unpack one dump and compare it with the commit it holds | | `--at` | the newest | with `--restore-test`, which snapshot to restore | | `--manifest` | — | do not back up: regenerate the dumps repo's `manifest.json` from its tree | ## The manifest is derived, not written by hand `/manifest.json` is regenerated from the dumps repository's own tree — after every backup, and on demand: ```bash GITHUB_TOKEN=... python3 backup.py --manifest --dumps dumps ``` It was hand-written once, on the store's first day, and never again: it went on claiming one repository was backed up while the store held 78. A derived index cannot drift, and if it is wrong then the tree it was derived from is wrong too. It is verified on the way in exactly as a dump is — the stored blob sha is compared with the sha of the bytes written — and a manifest that cannot be written **fails the run**, because a derived index allowed to go stale quietly is the defect this replaces. The one thing it does not record is the commit each dump holds. That is inside the tarball; `--restore-test` reads it. ## Proving a backup can actually be restored A backup that ran is not a backup that restores. This unpacks one dump and compares it, file for file, with the commit the dump names — every file's git blob sha against the repository's own tree at that commit. It exits 0 only on an exact match: ```bash GITHUB_TOKEN=... python3 backup.py --restore-test --repo drsamonline/forge GITHUB_TOKEN=... python3 backup.py --restore-test --repo drsamonline/forge --at 2026-10-27T124846Z ``` ``` read 0.69 MB; the API's stored blob sha is 81bbcaf0af unpacks clean (gzip CRC verified): 349 files, taken at 57d64d93c932 PASS EXACT RESTORE - 349 files match drsamonline/forge@57d64d93c932 file for file ``` It also fails on a truncated dump, on a dump whose top directory names a different repository, and on a tree GitHub truncated — an incomplete comparison is never a pass. Run it from the workflow by dispatching `backup` with `restore_test: true`. ## Verified ``` python3 tests/test_backup.py 50 passed, 0 failed ``` The tests cover the decisions that must be right — rotation keeps the newest N and deletes the oldest, the timestamp sorts chronologically, and a **full dumps repo rolls over to a new one**. Disabling rotation makes **4** of them fail. ## Licence MIT. (c) 2026 Dr Sohil Momin. Part of the Forge system.

# Base Bench

<!-- shot:start -->

![Screenshot](docs/shot.png)

<!-- shot:end -->

[![live](https://img.shields.io/badge/live-online-22c55e)](https://drsamonline.github.io/base-bench/play/)
[![test](https://github.com/drsamonline/base-bench/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/drsamonline/base-bench/actions/workflows/test.yml)
[![License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-informational)](LICENSE)
[![download](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/drsamonline/base-bench

**Every number base, unit and timezone on one page — with the working shown.**

Master list **#142** · built from `QUEUE/app-base-bench.md`.

A converter you cannot check is a converter you have to trust. Base Bench shows
the arithmetic at every step, so the answer is verifiable on paper.

## What it does

- **Number bases, linked.** Decimal, hex, binary and octal are four views of one
  number: type in any field and the other three follow, with no reload. Plus any
  base from 2 to 36, and a digit strip so you can see what is legal.
- **The working, in the base you typed into.** 255 → hex is shown as
  `255 / 16 = 15 remainder 15 (F)`, `15 / 16 = 0 remainder 15 (F)`, then *read the
  remainders bottom-up: FF*. That is the sum you would do by hand.
- **Units**, with the factor printed: length, mass, data and time, plus
  temperature (which is affine, so it gets its own formula rather than a factor).
  `KB` and `KiB` are kept apart, because they are different units.
- **Timezones** by fixed offset, with the day rollover stated rather than
  swallowed: 01:00 IST is 19:30 UTC **the previous day**.
- **A log** of the conversions you keep, on the device, exportable as CSV.

## What it refuses to do

It is not a scientific calculator. It converts, and it shows how. It also
refuses to invent an answer: an illegal digit, an unknown unit, a length
converted to a mass, or `0x` on base 10 each produce a sentence saying what is
wrong, not a plausible-looking number.

## Run it

Open `docs/play/index.html`. That is the whole app — the kits it uses
(`web-kit.js`, `export-kit.js`) sit next to it, so it works from `file://` and
from GitHub Pages, with no build step and no network.

## The proof

`node test-node.js` — **91 assertions**, no dependencies. The engine is
`docs/play/basebench.js` and the page is a view over it, so testing the engine
tests what the app does. Included are the spec's own done-means (255 shows as
`FF` and `11111111` in the same view, and typing into any field updates the
others), 4,004 round trips across bases 2, 8, 16 and 36, the temperature
fixed-points, and the timezone day rollover.

Each assertion was checked to **bite**: five mutations of the engine (lowercase
digits, the day rollover removed, the `- 32` dropped from the Fahrenheit formula,
the prefix check disabled, the digits reversed) each fail between 1 and 9
assertions.

## Licence

PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 — free for any noncommercial purpose. Commercial use
needs a licence from the author. See [`LICENSE`](LICENSE).

Commercial use requires a paid licence from the author — see [`NOTICE.md`](NOTICE.md).

# BlinkCode AI ![Screenshot](docs/shot.png) **Point your camera, get the file.** A file is compressed into a compact *File DNA* container, painted as **SpectraCode colour matrices**, and recovered by pointing a camera at the sender's screen — no server, no network after the first launch. [![License: PolyForm Noncommercial](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-PolyForm%20Noncommercial%201.0.0-7c3aed)](LICENSE) [![Commercial licence](https://img.shields.io/badge/commercial-licence%20available-22c55e)](COMMERCIAL.md) [![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai)](https://github.com/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai/commits) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai)](https://github.com/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai/stargazers) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/github/downloads/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai/total)](https://github.com/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai/releases) [![PWA: offline-first](https://img.shields.io/badge/PWA-offline--first-06b6d4)](https://drsamonline.github.io/blinkcode-ai/play/) [![No runtime deps](https://img.shields.io/badge/runtime%20deps-0-6366f1)](package.json) **[Live demo](https://drsamonline.github.io/blinkcode-ai/play/)**  ·  **[Landing page](https://drsamonline.github.io/blinkcode-ai/)**  ·  **[All projects](https://drsamonline.github.io/)** **Download:** [Windows (.exe)](https://github.com/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai/releases/latest/download/blinkcode-ai-portable.exe)  ·  [Android (.apk)](https://github.com/drsamonline/blinkcode-ai/releases/latest/download/blinkcode-ai.apk)
--- BlinkCode AI is the **high-capacity** member of the optical-transfer family. Where a QR code carries black-and-white modules, a SpectraCode carries **colour cells** — five bits per cell instead of one — so a single frame holds kilobytes rather than hundreds of bytes. ``` file ─▶ arithmetic coder ─▶ File DNA ─▶ frames ─▶ RS(255,223) ─▶ colour grid │ file ◀─ arithmetic decoder ◀─ CRC-32 ◀─ collector ◀─ RS ◀──────┘ ▲ camera ─▶ bullseye detect ─▶ homography ─▶ colour correction ─▶ classify ``` ## What it does - **SpectraCode transport** — a 36-colour palette, 5 bits/cell, bullseye markers and a calibration strip, rendered at two densities (120×80 and 60×40). - **Real compression** — an order-1 arithmetic coder **with a match (LZP) model**, plus a perceptual image mode. See the benchmark below. - **Reed-Solomon RS(255,223)** — repairs up to 16 damaged bytes per block, which is what lets a frame survive glare, shadow and mis-classified cells. - **Full optical decoder** — marker detection → homography → 3×4 colour correction → cell classification → RS, all in a Web Worker. - **Rateless (fountain) frame stream** — an LT code with a systematic prefix, so the receiver rebuilds the container from *any* k + a little overhead symbols. A missed frame costs one more symbol, not a whole loop. CRC-32 verifies the result. - **Offline-first PWA** — the model bundle is downloaded once and cached; after that the app never touches the network. ## Compression benchmark `npm run bench` — the arithmetic coder with and without the match model, against gzip. Measured on the project's own corpora: | corpus | orig | order-1 | + match | gzip | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | english prose (repeated) | 18 000 | 6.6× | **53.9×** | 136× | | english prose (varied) | 14 379 | 2.6× | **12.5×** | 13.3× | | JSON records | 71 556 | 4.0× | **8.6×** | 15.5× | | source code | 102 286 | 2.1× | **2.9×** | 3.3× | | already-compressed (gzip) | 156 | 1.3× | **2.0×** | 1.8× | | random bytes | 16 000 | 0.93× | 0.92× | 1.00× | | **total** | **222 377** | **2.4×** | **3.5×** | 4.2× | The match model added **~31%** overall over the original order-1 coder. It is still beaten by gzip on long repeats, and cannot beat entropy — see the honest limits below. ## Robustness `npm run robustness` pushes a simulated camera (perspective tilt, colour cast, vignetting, blur, sensor noise) until the decoder breaks. Current margins on a standard-density code: | condition | still decodes up to | | --- | --- | | sensor noise | ±32 (8-bit levels) | | blur | a 3-pixel box radius | | low light (gain) | 0.3× – 1.0× | The decoder samples each cell with a **median** (robust to edge bleed and glare), stretches the capture's contrast before binarising, and tries several thresholds when locating the bullseye markers. ## Perceptual mode The lossy image mode quantises a photo into a 64-value latent. `npm run perceptual` measures reconstruction error: | image | RMSE | PSNR | | --- | ---: | ---: | | smooth gradient | 3.9 | 36.3 dB | | photo-like | 7.7 | 30.4 dB | | 2-pixel stripes | 57.5 | 12.9 dB | The last row is the honest limit: a 64-value latent cannot represent near-Nyquist detail, and no reconstruction trick brings it back. Reconstruction now uses a **bicubic** upscale — bilinear left visible faceting on gradients and cost about 9 dB there. ## Honest limits These matter more than the pitch, so they are stated plainly here and in the app's "How it works" tab: - **One SpectraCode frame holds 5,111 payload bytes** (1,097 in robust density). Throughput is roughly `5 KB × frame rate` — about 15 KB/s at 3 fps. Frames are rateless, so a missed frame costs an extra symbol rather than a full loop. - **1000:1 lossless compression of arbitrary files is impossible.** Lossless coding cannot go below the entropy of the data. Real measured ratios are in the table above: strong on structured text, ~1× on already-compressed data. - **Extreme ratios exist only in perceptual mode**, which is genuinely lossy — an image becomes a 64-value latent and returns as a soft reconstruction. - **The "neural" model is a mock with a real interface.** The bundle format, one-time download, offline caching and the coder's model API are production shaped; the weights are trained order-1 statistics plus DCT quantiser scales (~129 KB), not a large neural net. `Order1Model` in `src/lib/arith.js`, `Order1MatchModel` in `src/lib/predict.js` and the transforms in `src/lib/image-codec.js` are the swap points. - **Camera decoding is validated in simulation**, not against physical phone optics: the tests render a code, apply perspective tilt, a colour cast and vignetting, and decode it end to end. Real-world glare, motion blur and low-end sensors may still need per-cell voting and multi-frame averaging. ## Run it ```bash npm install npm run build:model # (re)train and package the downloadable model bundle npm run serve # http://localhost:8080 npm test # codec + full optical loopback tests npm run bench # compression benchmark npm run lint ``` Open the app, pick a file (or paste text), hit **Compress**, then **Show SpectraCode** on the sender and **Start scanning** on the receiver. Without a second device, the **loopback self-test** pushes every rendered frame back through the real optical decoder. ## Project layout ``` src/ index.html app.js styles.css sw.js manifest.webmanifest lib/ arith.js arithmetic coder + order-1 model predict.js order-1 + match (LZP) model — the compression upgrade codec.js File DNA encode/decode orchestration format.js container header fountain.js LT fountain codes (rateless frame stream) image-codec.js perceptual latent encoder/decoder geometry.js linear solver, homography, colour-correction fit palette.js the 36 reference colours rs.js Reed-Solomon GF(256) spectracode.js layout, symbol packing, renderer spectra-decode.js marker detection → payload bytes storage.js one-time model download + offline persistence stream.js frame header, CRC-32, out-of-order frame collector surface.js canvas / buffer drawing targets workers/ model loader, compression, decompression, optical decode models/ucg-v1.bin downloadable model bundle tools/ build.js, build-model.js, bench.js, tune.js, robustness.js, perceptual.js, update-scales.js, serve.js tests/ codec, stream, predict + end-to-end optical loopback docs/ landing page + built demo (GitHub Pages) ``` ## Licence BlinkCode AI is **free for personal, academic, hobby and non-profit use** under the [PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0](LICENSE). **Commercial use needs a paid licence** — see [COMMERCIAL.md](COMMERCIAL.md). ## Credits Built by **Dr Sohil Momin** ([@drsamonline](https://github.com/drsamonline)).
